title: The Best Lesson in Didactics
author: Norma Sancho
summary: Sancho writes as a mature student partway through a teaching degree, reviewing a Fundamentals of Didactics course and finding that the most instructive thing in it was not on the syllabus. Much of the essay is a complaint about the discipline's habit of hedging, where every claim arrives wrapped in caveats and context until, as she puts it, didactics seems to ask permission to be a discipline at all. She sets against this her admiration for writers who assert things and then defend them, naming Szasz and the antinatalists Benatar and Cabrera as examples of the nerve she finds missing in education scholarship. The essay's strongest passage is an analogy with acting, where technique alone cannot manufacture presence but presence without technique collapses into gimmickry, which she applies directly to teaching method. The turn comes when her professor emails unprompted to explain a question she had answered wrongly on a midterm, the first time in sixteen months of study that any instructor had contacted her personally. Sancho treats that small gesture as the real lesson in didactics, since it converted her from a platform user into a student more effectively than the course's four laws and five principles had. The piece is worth keeping as a student's eye account of how thin the relational layer of online teacher training can be.
points: Sancho's central complaint is methodological rather than personal, that education scholarship hedges every assertion into subjectivity and so makes it hard to teach anything as a settled certainty.
Her acting analogy does the argumentative work, holding that technique channels presence rather than creating it, so method alone never accounts for the teachers students remember.
She reports that the discipline came alive for her only when a professor sent an unsolicited email correcting a wrong midterm answer, the first such contact since she began the program in May 2025.

The piece doubles as a critique of passive online delivery, describing a first live class spent on seven minutes of the instructor's credentials followed by a monologue with cameras and microphones off.
quotes: I completed the course I was most looking forward to: Fundamentals of Didactics. I took it for granted that this subject would lay the groundwork for doing what a teacher is supposed to do: teach.

My only complaint regarding this subject is that, like the others, it quickly strips away any idealized view of the profession and its practice. That has been the pattern throughout every course. We are constantly—almost ritually—reminded not to state anything without surrounding it with caveats, contexts, perspectives, historical nuances, and, frequently, apologies.

It also serves as a compass for teaching practice: what to select and in what order; which activities and resources to employ; how to adapt the process to the student and the context; and what evidence will indicate whether learning has actually taken place.

It follows, then, that an intense personality lacking technique can result in mere gimmickry, whereas impeccable technique lacking presence can yield a performance that is technically correct yet forgettable.

A similar dynamic applies to teachers. Methodology does not automatically generate a distinctive voice, sensitivity, humor, intellectual authority, or the ability to sense the group dynamic; however, it enables those qualities to be translated into pedagogical decisions: when to explain, when to ask questions, when to remain silent, how to sequence the difficulty of a topic, when to abandon the lesson plan, and how to verify student understanding.

I put it that way because what I remember are decent people who were weary, pressured employees—and, as I now realize, overworked and underpaid. Bureaucrats with a license to teach. They were intolerant, dry in their explanations, and unable to connect with students as individuals.
This gesture, which came as a complete surprise to me, made me feel that there is a professor who pays attention to what I do; that I’m not just a user of the platform, but a student.
Tonight she’s teaching her first live class. And tonight, even if the monologue happens again, for the first time I’ll be attending class with a real teacher who treated me as a student.
